title: Sense of harmony, chord changes and modulation
summary: St. Cyr explains how he thought through chord changes, found harmonizing chords, and modulated smoothly; compares with Ed Garland on bass.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I'm wondering, say when you played dances, even after you learned to read or before, whenever you played a lot of pieces, as soon as the leader calls the piece, tells you what key it's in, or maybe they didn't even always tell you what key it's in. Did you start thinking about, I have to play the C card for four measures and I change to F and I go to G and the B flat seven? Well, yes. Those things come in your mind? Yes.
That's right. Well, I never knew the value of measures, but I had a sense of rhythm and I might put it this way, just how far I should go in a certain key.
Did you think now the next card is going to come, I have to change to G or A?
Absolutely.
That was, you didn't just start playing and your fingers find the... No, no.
You had it in here.
You had to be thinking all the time.
Absolutely. Yes, sir. And I'll tell you that I had a sense of harmony, a natural sense of harmony. That's the one thing that made me become so popular.
That's right. Yeah, a lot of people play the wrong chords.
Because, yes, they play a major where a minor should be, or a minor where a major should be, or where I play C, A7, D7, G7. A guy would play, the other guys would play just C and G7.
Simplified, doesn't it? Yes, I know. It doesn't always harmonize. Two cards.

But I always tried to find chords that would harmonize. And try to find as many changes that would harmonize with the number as possible. I always had that natural sense of harmony. And that's the one thing that made me very popular as a guitar player. Because guys had been playing with the very, guys that were supposed to be famous in those days, Joe Brooks and Rene Baptiste. And those people, when I played the number I found so many changes in between what they played, that the guys wondered how I played it and didn't read. I just had a natural sense of harmony, I could feel it. And at one time I could modulate. You see now the bands play a number and they change keys, they just jump down from one key to the other. But in those days we used to modulate to the key. You modulate about four meshes or eight meshes into the next key, working to gradually. And I used to modulate from any key.
From C to A flat.

See guys playing the number and C and he want to fall to A flat, he just drop down in A flat with both feet. See he ain't got the courtesy enough to modulate. It's much smoother when you. Oh yeah, when you just work into it.
They're double measures, number three. That's right.
And man, I used to make chords and just work right in the front seat, work right on into A flat. See. I'm rusty on that now because the bands doesn't do it anymore. See.

But at one time you've written all those out, I mean the B, A flat, C, and you've actually written out on paper, not the actual notes, but I mean your succession of chords. Yes, uh-huh, succession of chords. You really thought that in your mind. Absolutely, that was in here. And your fingers didn't just start to go along. No, no, no. You're thinking about something else.
No, no, that was in the mind. Yes, yeah. A little mind.

Because I was asking for instance, Ed Garland, in playing his bass, in which he doesn't have the same problem quite as you playing the chords. No. But they do play chords on the bass too, you know. Oh yes. And I asked him if he was conscious of the chords as he played them and he said no, hardly ever. He said I could be talking to somebody. And he'd be playing his bass and yet his fingers would find the right chords on any piece that he knew. He never, as he knew a piece, he never thought of what chord he or even what key it was in.
Well, I, there's lots of guys can do that.
I never could.
You always actually thought of what I'm doing.
I'm always conscious of what I'm doing. How's the thing you had on the guitar with all those strings?
